description: Width tiers for Languages — Background Language Learner Pathway, Years 5–6 band
subject: Languages — Background Language Learner

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term at Y5-6. For communicating descriptors: the minimum range of task types and contexts in which the capability is demonstrated. For understanding descriptors: the minimum range of language features, text structures or cultural phenomena engaged with.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope from ACARA elaborations — what a well-taught Y5-6 background language learner class would have engaged with across the breadth of the descriptor.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new task contexts (communicating) or new language/cultural phenomena (understanding). At Y5-6, authentic community connections and intercultural comparison are primary width directions.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations for the Chinese Background Language Learner pathway (Y5-6) used as source data. Chinese-specific references are preserved as representative examples of the generic target-language principle.

AC9LCH6C01.minimum_width: Express at least two opinions on a topic and respond to a peer's view with at least one agreement or disagreement expression; demonstrate at least two active listening strategies during a sustained exchange of at least five turns.
AC9LCH6C01.typical_width: Exchange ideas and opinions in class discussions; express agreement, disagreement and qualification; use active listening strategies — interjections, non-verbal cues, follow-up questions; express gratitude, sympathy and concern; exchange information about personal experiences, recent events and future plans through face-to-face and digital formats.
wider: Participate in an exchange on a topic introduced spontaneously by the partner — demonstrate real-time adaptation to an unplanned direction across at least six turns
Record and review a sustained conversation — identify specific moments where active listening strategies were or should have been deployed and discuss the effect on the exchange
Compare active listening and opinion-exchange conventions in the target language with Australian English — identify where the conventions are similar and where they are culturally specific
elaborations: initiating and sustaining conversations including face-to-face and secure online conversations by asking peers about personal interests
playing guessing games and practising modelled sentences and question words
developing conversation skills such as staying on topic, recognising non-verbal cues and using interjections
exchanging ideas and opinions in class discussions, expressing agreement, disagreement, negotiating and demonstrating active listening
using secure digital resources to write a daily or weekly journal recording events or highlights
expressing gratitude, apologies, sympathy or concern when interacting with family, friends or peers
checking on the progress of others during learning tasks using questions
exchanging text messages and emails using appropriate formats to negotiate weekend plans

AC9LCH6C02.minimum_width: Use at least three language structures for suggesting, agreeing, or resolving during a collaborative task; participate in planning a shared project with at least three target language turns including at least one suggestion.
AC9LCH6C02.typical_width: Use a range of planning and negotiation language — suggestions, responses, alternatives, agreements, resolutions; use idiomatic expressions in collaborative contexts; collaborate to plan school events, community presentations and campaigns; provide feedback on peers' contributions; use target language throughout planning processes.
wider: Lead a collaborative planning discussion — facilitating justification-based decision-making and managing competing proposals to a shared outcome
Compare how suggestions, disagreements and negotiations are managed in collaborative contexts in the target language community with Australian conventions
Research and arrange a visit by an expert from the target language community to share knowledge and promote language learning
elaborations: planning and collaborating in shared activities such as running a school assembly in the target language
participating in planning and presentation of a role-play with peers, such as an imagined trip, discussing preferences and bargaining
listening to or viewing community media and participating in advertised activities
collaborating to decide on a menu for a class lunch and negotiating items, prices and delivery
contributing to the development of a set of class rules
providing feedback about peer presentations using modelled language
collaboratively writing a children's story and reading it to younger learners
planning a campaign for a school or community event by creating digital posters or pamphlets
researching and arranging a visit by an expert to share knowledge and promote language learning in the school community

AC9LCH6C03.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of language variation (tone, register, word choice) in a text and explain what each suggests about purpose or audience; produce at least one response demonstrating a deliberate language or format choice appropriate to audience or purpose.
AC9LCH6C03.typical_width: Identify perspective, language variation, setting and character in texts; analyse how language choices reflect purpose and audience; respond to informative and imaginative texts in different ways for different purposes; compare information across texts; respond to First Nations Australian stories in English in target language; use target language in research and presentation contexts.
wider: Compare how the same topic is represented in two different target language texts — identify differences in perspective, language choices and what is emphasised or omitted
Listen to or read First Nations Australian authors' stories in English and respond through a range of text types in the target language, reflecting on cultural perspectives
Interview family or peers to collect stories of migration to Australia — identify words and expressions that reflect important cultural values and present findings for a specific audience
elaborations: listening to, reading or viewing informative texts and discussing opinions
identifying and describing key elements of informative or imaginative texts by asking and responding to questions
reading or viewing imaginative texts and performing scenes illustrating aspects of a character's attitude or emotion
listening to or viewing First Nations Australian authors' stories in English and responding to them in a range of text types in Chinese
researching, comparing and presenting information about aspects of life in China and Australia
identifying variations in aspects of language use such as tone, gesture and word choice in different contexts
interviewing family, friends or peers to collect stories of migration, identifying words and expressions that reflect important values
reading extracts from culturally significant children's literature and discussing personal responses
illustrating an extract of text by selecting images to express the content, mood or key message

AC9LCH6C04.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples where literal translation would be misleading and explain the correct interpretation strategy; compare the output of at least two translation approaches for the same text and identify at least two differences.
AC9LCH6C04.typical_width: Examine the risks of literal translation in expressions, idioms and proverbs; identify colloquial and slang expressions used by young people; apply strategies to interpret context-specific language; use and evaluate print and digital translation tools; create bilingual resources for school and community use.
wider: Translate a text containing idioms or culturally-embedded expressions, documenting each translation decision — explain why a direct translation was or was not possible
Create a bilingual resource for a real school or community event — evaluate its accuracy and appropriateness with a target audience member and revise
Compare the output of a digital translation tool with a human translation of the same text — identify differences and discuss what the human translator understood that the tool missed
elaborations: examining the risks of literal or word-for-word translation when translating expressions, idioms and proverbs
recognising different levels of formality in language and using language appropriate to context
interpreting examples of colloquialisms or slang typically used by young people
identifying context-specific language used in different settings such as supermarket, doctor or visiting a friend
creating and using bilingual resources for language learning, such as glossaries of cultural terms
reading children's stories in bilingual form and reflecting on ideas that may not be readily translated
using a range of resources to assist in creating a target language translation of a text
composing bilingual resources for the school community such as posters for class or school performances

AC9LCH6C05.minimum_width: Produce a text of at least eight sentences using at least three cohesive devices; create a text with at least two deliberate adaptations for a specific purpose or audience.
AC9LCH6C05.typical_width: Use a range of cohesive devices to sequence and develop information; create informative texts — community newsletters, travel brochures, procedures, presentations — adapted for purpose and audience; create and perform imaginative texts — scripted plays, modified folk tales, imagined interactions; use descriptive language and experiment with structure.
wider: Create the same content in two different formats for two different audiences — compare the language and format choices and explain how each serves its intended audience
Create a print or digital advertisement or brochure in the target language for travel to a First Nations Country/Place location, including what to see and do, means of travel and what to respect
Create a text for a real external audience — a community publication, school broadcast, or digital production — and seek and incorporate audience feedback
elaborations: working in teams to prepare a presentation supported by digital media
creating displays using graphics, photographs and illustrations to document and convey ideas
preparing and creating a video clip to share with peers overseas introducing aspects of local culture
creating a print or digital advertisement or brochure in Chinese for travel to a First Nations Country/Place location
explaining a procedure or practice to others, for example, community recycling, a recipe or eating etiquette
role-playing a modified well-known children's story
producing and performing short scripted plays, experimenting with descriptive language
composing and participating in imagined interactions with characters from familiar texts
writing a letter or creating a video for their future self
creating texts for a range of audiences and purposes for school or community newsletters

AC9LCH6U01.minimum_width: Read or say the same sentence with at least two different emotional registers demonstrating distinguishable intonation or stress changes; identify at least one tone change pattern and demonstrate correct application in at least three examples.
AC9LCH6U01.typical_width: Use intonation, stress and phrasing to express different emotions and registers; read lyrics, poems and news aloud with attention to tonal patterns; explore how intonation changes meaning; apply tone change patterns; use digital tools to check pronunciation and monitor own fluency; understand regional accent variation.
wider: Conduct a systematic self-review of a recorded spoken performance — identify specific tonal and intonation targets, practise, re-record and compare the two versions
Investigate the tonal and intonation patterns of a specific genre — for example, news broadcast versus conversation — and identify the genre-specific prosodic conventions
Compare how a specific emotional register is conveyed through intonation differently across the target language and English
elaborations: reading the lyrics of Chinese pop songs, modelled texts, tongue twisters, poems and news aloud with attention to tones and pronunciation
using digital tools to check the correct pronunciation of Chinese and using voice-recording apps to check own tone and intonation
recognising syllable changes in speech, including change of tonal value
recognising how tone marks affect pronunciation and meaning
playing speaking games to demonstrate different emotions using features of pronunciation
understanding that Chinese has different regional accents spoken by people in different provinces and communities

AC9LCH6U02.minimum_width: Infer the meaning of at least three unfamiliar words using component or morphological knowledge; produce a text of at least ten sentences applying writing system conventions and at least three complex grammatical structures.
AC9LCH6U02.typical_width: Analyse characters through component examples; use digital tools for pronunciation lookup; infer meaning from known morphemes; understand character formation types; use appropriate punctuation; build complex messages using conjunctions, sequence words and comparative structures; discriminate contextual meanings of polysemous characters; apply aspect markers and tense expression.
wider: Investigate a semantic field and identify the morphological patterns that link characters across the field
Compose a text on a genuinely unfamiliar topic using morphological inference and contextual strategies — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Compare how a specific grammatical function (aspect, comparison, conditionality) is handled differently in the target language and English
elaborations: analysing common simple and compound characters through multiple examples and identifying placement of radicals
using digital tools to write a specific character and obtain pronunciation using online dictionaries
developing understanding of types of Chinese characters such as pictographs and phono-semantic characters
inferring meaning of unfamiliar words from known morphemes
using appropriate punctuation in writing
exploring and building more complex messages using joining words, conjunction words and sequence words
discriminating between contextual meanings of characters with multiple meanings
using the function of words and structures in language to indicate completion of action
understanding different applications of grammatical rules in spoken and written language
exploring ways to express similarities and comparatives

AC9LCH6U03.minimum_width: Compare at least two grammatical features across target language and English using metalanguage, explaining where the two languages work similarly and where they differ; analyse the structure of at least one text type in both languages and identify at least three differences.
AC9LCH6U03.typical_width: Compare grammatical features using metalanguage — passive and active voice, tense encoding, adjectival verbs, cohesive devices; compare structural features of familiar text types across the two languages; create comparative vocabulary lists; explore how tenses and sequence words function differently across the two languages.
wider: Compare essay organisation conventions in the target language with English — identify where the author's position appears, how evidence is marshalled, and discuss what this reveals about cultural epistemological conventions
Produce two versions of the same text — one following target language conventions and one following English conventions — and compare the structural and linguistic differences
Create a bilingual grammar comparison resource for a specific feature — designed to be used by another learner of one of the two languages
elaborations: discussing aspects of grammar using metalanguage in Chinese or English
identifying and comparing language features of different text types in Chinese and English
comparing the use of passive voice and active voice in Chinese and English
comparing structural features of familiar personal, informative and imaginative texts
comparing different types of texts such as recipes, songs, stories and recounts
creating comparative lists of vocabulary used in different contexts
understanding how to create textual cohesion using adverbs of sequence and conjunctions
recognising grammatical features and how their use differs in Chinese and English
comparing the use of tenses in Chinese and English

AC9LCH6U04.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of language choices reflecting cultural values, and explain the impact on an interaction; reflect on at least one experience of navigating between two cultural-language contexts.
AC9LCH6U04.typical_width: Examine how language choices across contexts reflect cultural values; discuss how the same interaction would be managed differently across cultural contexts; identify regional variation in language; reflect on how interacting in the target language feels different from English; explore how First Nations Australian languages and target language communities both connect language to cultural belonging.
wider: Explore in Chinese or English how First Nations Australian language and cultural practices connect language to Country/Place, and compare with how the target language connects to community and cultural identity

Research how the target language is used in the local community and compare with how it is used in a different regional or national community — identify specific differences and discuss what they reveal about cultural diversity
Reflect on a specific experience of cultural miscommunication — identify the cultural values at play, what was assumed, what caused difficulty, and what was learned
elaborations: discussing language choices expected or required in diverse contexts across languages
recognising the interconnections between cultural practices and language use
noticing that language varies between regions
exploring in Chinese and English how language and culture are expressed through First Nations Australians' song, dance or artworks
identifying ways in which Chinese language and culture influence the lives of Australians
engaging with Chinese peers in diverse contexts and exploring strategies to overcome miscommunication
noticing and reflecting on how interacting in Chinese may feel different from interacting in English
